subject: Bio
title: Coordination, inheritance & variation
sub: Nerves and the eye, hormones and tropisms, chromosomes and genes, variation and natural selection
strategyIntro: Cambridge Core Biology is assessed on Paper 1 (40 multiple-choice questions, 45 min), Paper 3 (structured theory questions, 1h 15, 80 marks) and Paper 6 (questions on experiments). Your school test may be shorter, but it will be marked the same way.

strategy.title: Multiple choice
points: About a minute per question. If one is taking longer, mark it and move on.
Cross out options you know are wrong first. Two often look similar: read every word.
Never leave one blank. A wrong answer loses nothing.

strategy.title: Structured questions
points: Marks go to keywords. Write the textbook term: “oviduct”, not “tube”.
The marks in brackets tell you how many separate points to make.
Label diagrams with a ruler line that touches the exact part.

strategy.title: Questions on experiments
points: Results tables: units go in the column headings, not next to each number.
Graphs: label both axes with units, choose an even scale, plot with small crosses.
Know the control variables and one safety precaution for each experiment.

strategy.title: Easy marks people lose
points: Saying nerves carry “messages”. Say electrical impulses along neurones.
Writing “the pupil contracts”. The iris muscles contract; the pupil gets smaller (constricts).
In genetics, using the same letter in two different ways: one letter, capital for dominant, lower case for recessive.
Writing that organisms “adapt” or “choose” to change. Individuals with useful variations survive and pass on their alleles.

commandWords: Give a short fact. No explanation needed.
Say what happens or what you see. With data, quote figures and units.
Say why or how. Use “because” and link cause to effect.
Apply what you know to a new situation. Any sensible reason scores.
Give similarities or differences for both things in the same sentence.
Show working and give the unit.
quizIntro: Answer in Paper 1 style: about a minute each, eliminating wrong options first. Read the explanation after every answer, even when you get it right.
flashIntro: These are close to Cambridge’s own wording. Say each definition out loud before you tap, then check you used the exact keywords.

flashcards.back: Central nervous system (brain and spinal cord) plus peripheral nervous system (nerves). Coordinates and regulates body functions.
An electrical signal that passes along neurones.
Sensory neurones (from receptors), relay neurones (in the CNS), motor neurones (to effectors).
A fast, automatic response to a stimulus, without conscious thought. Protects the body.
Stimulus → receptor → sensory neurone → relay neurone → motor neurone → effector (muscle or gland) → response.
Groups of receptor cells that respond to specific stimuli: light, sound, touch, temperature, chemicals.
Both refract (bend) light; the lens focuses it onto the retina.
The retina contains light-sensitive receptor cells; the optic nerve carries impulses to the brain.
Coloured ring of muscle that controls the size of the pupil, and so how much light enters the eye.
Bright light: the pupil gets smaller to protect the retina. Dim light: the pupil gets wider to let more light in.
A chemical substance made by a gland and carried by the blood, which changes the activity of specific target organs.
Adrenal glands: adrenaline. Pancreas: insulin. Testes: testosterone. Ovaries: oestrogen.
Released in “fight or flight” situations: increases heart rate and breathing rate and widens the pupils.
Nerves: electrical impulses, very fast, short-lived. Hormones: chemicals in the blood, slower, longer-lasting.
The maintenance of a constant internal environment.
Made by the pancreas; lowers the concentration of glucose in the blood.
About 37 °C. When hot we sweat; evaporation of sweat cools the skin. When cold we shiver.
A response in which parts of a plant grow towards or away from the direction of light.
A response in which parts of a plant grow towards or away from gravity.
Shoots grow towards light and away from gravity. Roots grow towards gravity.
The passing on of genetic information from one generation to the next.
A thread-like structure of DNA, carrying genetic information in the form of genes.
A length of DNA that codes for a protein.
An alternative form of a gene, e.g. the alleles for blue or brown eyes.
Body cells have 46 chromosomes (23 pairs). Gametes have 23.
Females are XX, males XY. Eggs all carry X; sperm carry X or Y, so there is a 50% chance of each sex.
Genotype: the alleles an organism has (e.g. Bb). Phenotype: its observable features (e.g. brown eyes).
A dominant allele shows whenever it is present (capital letter). A recessive allele only shows when there are two copies.
Homozygous: two identical alleles (BB or bb). Heterozygous: two different alleles (Bb).
Mitosis makes genetically identical cells (growth, repair). Meiosis makes gametes with half the chromosomes, genetically different.
Differences between individuals of the same species.
A range of phenotypes between two extremes, e.g. height or mass. Caused by genes and the environment.
A few distinct phenotypes with no in-betweens, e.g. ABO blood group. Usually caused by genes alone.
A genetic change. Source of new alleles. Rate increased by ionising radiation and some chemicals.
An inherited feature that helps an organism survive and reproduce in its environment.
e.g. cactus: spines instead of leaves, thick waxy cuticle, stores water in its stem, long or wide roots.
Variation → more offspring than can survive → competition → best adapted survive and reproduce → pass on their alleles.
A mutation lets a few bacteria survive an antibiotic; they reproduce, so the resistant population grows.
Humans choose individuals with useful features to breed, and repeat over many generations.
In natural selection the environment does the selecting; in selective breeding humans do.

quiz.q: Which neurone carries impulses from a receptor to the central nervous system?
quiz.why: Sensory neurones carry impulses into the CNS; motor neurones carry them out to effectors.

quiz.q: Which is the correct order in a reflex arc?
options: Receptor, motor neurone, relay neurone, sensory neurone, effector
Effector, sensory neurone, relay neurone, motor neurone, receptor
Receptor, sensory neurone, relay neurone, motor neurone, effector
Receptor, relay neurone, sensory neurone, effector, motor neurone
quiz.why: Receptor → sensory → relay (in spinal cord) → motor → effector.

quiz.q: What happens to the pupil in bright light?
quiz.why: The pupil narrows so less light reaches the retina and damages it.

quiz.q: Which part of the eye contains the light-sensitive cells?
quiz.why: The retina has the receptor cells. The cornea and lens focus light onto it.

quiz.q: In the knee-jerk reflex, what is the effector?
quiz.why: The effector carries out the response: the thigh muscle contracts and the leg kicks.

quiz.q: How are hormones carried around the body?
quiz.why: Hormones are secreted into the blood and travel to their target organs.

quiz.q: Which is an effect of adrenaline?
quiz.why: Adrenaline prepares the body for action: faster heart rate and breathing, wider pupils.

quiz.q: A plant on a windowsill grows towards the window. This is:
quiz.why: Growing towards light is positive phototropism.

quiz.q: Roots grow downwards. This response is called:
quiz.why: Roots grow towards gravity: positive gravitropism. Shoots show negative gravitropism.

quiz.q: Compared with nervous control, hormonal control is:
quiz.why: Hormones travel in the blood, so they act more slowly, but their effects last longer.

quiz.q: What is an allele?
options: A length of DNA that codes for a protein
An alternative form of a gene
quiz.why: A gene can come in different versions; each version is an allele.

quiz.q: Why does the father’s sperm decide the sex of a baby?
options: Sperm carry either an X or a Y chromosome
quiz.why: Every egg has an X. A sperm with X gives a girl (XX); a sperm with Y gives a boy (XY).

quiz.q: An organism has the genotype Tt. It is:
quiz.why: Two different alleles make it heterozygous. It shows the dominant (T) feature.

quiz.q: Bb is crossed with bb. What proportion of the offspring will be bb?
quiz.why: Gametes B or b from one parent, only b from the other: Bb, Bb, bb, bb. Half are bb.

quiz.q: How many chromosomes are in a human egg cell?
quiz.why: Gametes have half the number of body cells, so that fertilisation restores 46.

quiz.q: Two parents are both Bb (B = brown eyes, dominant). What is the chance of a child with blue eyes (bb)?
quiz.why: Offspring: BB, Bb, Bb, bb. One in four is bb.

quiz.q: Which is an example of discontinuous variation?
quiz.why: Blood group has a few distinct categories. The others vary across a continuous range.

quiz.q: Which increases the rate of mutation?
quiz.why: Ionising radiation (e.g. X-rays, gamma rays) and some chemicals damage DNA.

quiz.q: A farmer breeds only from the cows that give the most milk. This is:
quiz.why: Humans are choosing which animals breed, so it is selective (artificial) breeding.

quiz.q: Which graph is best for showing continuous variation, such as height?
quiz.why: Continuous data are grouped into ranges, plotted as a histogram with bars touching.

quiz.q: In natural selection, which individuals pass on their alleles?
options: The best adapted ones, which survive and reproduce
quiz.why: Individuals with helpful variations are more likely to survive long enough to breed.

examIntro: Paper 3 style. Write your answer first, then open the mark scheme and give yourself one mark per point you made clearly. One point per mark is the rule.

exam.q: State the function of (a) the lens and (b) the retina.
points: (a) Focuses light onto the retina
(b) Contains light-sensitive receptor cells / detects light

exam.q: Describe and explain what happens to the pupil when a person walks from a dark room into bright sunlight.
points: Muscles in the iris contract (this is a reflex)
The pupil gets smaller
Less light enters the eye
This protects the retina from damage

exam.q: A person touches a hot plate and pulls their hand away. Describe how the reflex arc brings about this response.
points: Receptors in the skin detect the heat (stimulus)
Impulse travels along a sensory neurone
To a relay neurone in the spinal cord / CNS
Then along a motor neurone
To the effector, a muscle, which contracts
Hand is pulled away quickly, without thinking
A chemical substance made by a gland
Carried in the blood
Changes the activity of one or more target organs

exam.q: Describe three effects of adrenaline on the body and suggest why each is useful in a dangerous situation.
points: Heart rate increases: more oxygen and glucose to muscles
Breathing rate increases: more oxygen taken in
Pupils widen: more light enters, better vision
Blood glucose rises: more fuel for respiration

exam.q: A bean seedling is laid on its side in the dark. Describe and explain how its shoot and root respond after a few days.
points: Shoot grows upwards
Negative gravitropism
Root grows downwards
Positive gravitropism
It is dark, so the response is to gravity, not light
Helps the shoot reach light and the root reach water / anchor the plant

exam.q: Define the terms gene and allele.
points: Gene: a length of DNA that codes for a protein
Allele: an alternative form of a gene

exam.q: Explain, using a genetic diagram, why there is an equal chance of a baby being a boy or a girl.
points: Mother is XX, father is XY
All eggs carry X
Half the sperm carry X and half carry Y
Diagram showing offspring XX, XX, XY, XY
So 1:1 ratio / 50% chance of each

exam.q: In humans, the allele for brown eyes (B) is dominant to the allele for blue eyes (b). Two heterozygous parents have a child. Use a genetic diagram to find the probability that the child has blue eyes.
points: Parents’ genotypes: Bb × Bb
Gametes: B and b from each parent
Offspring genotypes: BB, Bb, Bb, bb
Phenotypes: 3 brown : 1 blue
Probability of blue eyes = 1/4 (25%, 0.25)
exam.note: One mark per point. Label each line of the diagram.

exam.q: State two differences between continuous and discontinuous variation.
points: Continuous: a range of values; discontinuous: distinct groups
Continuous: genes and environment; discontinuous: mainly genes
Continuous shown on a histogram; discontinuous on a bar chart
Examples: height (continuous), blood group (discontinuous)

exam.q: Describe how a farmer could use selective breeding to produce wheat with a higher yield.
points: Choose the plants with the highest yield
Breed (cross-pollinate) them together
Grow the seeds and again select the highest-yielding offspring
Repeat over many generations

exam.q: Explain how natural selection could lead to a population of rabbits with thicker fur in a cold climate.
points: Rabbits show variation in fur thickness
This variation is genetic / caused by mutation
More offspring are produced than can survive
Competition / the cold kills some rabbits
Rabbits with thicker fur are better adapted and survive
They reproduce
They pass the alleles for thick fur to their offspring
Over many generations most rabbits have thick fur
